Directions: Read the passage “The Clever Rooster” and then answer each question that follows.
Context: This story takes place in Togo, West Africa, where the people speak the Ewe language.
Title: The Clever Rooster
Author: by Marileta Robinson
Content: `text(One day)` a clever rooster was pecking in the road for his breakfast when he found a watch - a gold, ticking pocket watch. Now what good would a pocket watch be to a rooster? Roosters don't have pockets. And they already know exactly what time to crow to wake the sun.
“Ah, but with a watch,” thought this clever rooster, “I will be able to tell the time not just at sunrise, but `text(every hour)`. I will be the most important rooster in the village!”

The rooster found a piece of string, and after many unsuccessful tries, he managed to hang the watch around his neck. He even managed to wind the watch so that it would keep ticking. And because he was such a clever rooster, it didn't take him long to learn to read the `text(hours)`, although he did have trouble with `text(half-hours)` and `text(quarter-hours)`.
From then on, from sunrise to sunset, the rooster proudly strutted around his yard, crowing the `text(hour)`. All would have gone well, perhaps, if the rooster hadn't lived next door to Mr. Agbele.

Mr. Agbele was a quiet, serious man who spent his `text(hours)` studying. He had always liked to hear the rooster crow at daybreak because then he knew it was time to get up and read his beloved books. But when the rooster began trumpeting the time `text(hour)` after `text(hour)`, Mr. Agbele was distressed. He couldn't concentrate on his reading - he couldn't even think. His life was being ruined by the rooster's watch.

After a few `text(days)`, Mr. Agbele decided to talk to the rooster. “Surely such a clever rooster will listen to reason,” he thought. The next time he heard the rooster shout, “Efo deka!” (“It's `text(one)` o'clock!”), Mr. Agbele stuck his head out of his window and called, “Friend Rooster!”
“What is it, Friend Man?” said the rooster.

“I have noticed that you are behaving in a most unusual way,” said Mr. Agbele. “All the other roosters in the village, I believe, crow only at daybreak. You crow `text(every hour)` on the `text(hour)`. Surely it would be better if you behaved in a more roosterly way.”

The rooster puffed out his chest feathers and replied, “The other roosters crow only at daybreak because they do not have watches. Since I have a watch, it is my duty to tell the time the rest of the `text(day)`. Good `text(day)`, Friend Man.”

But Mr. Agbele did not intend to give up so easily. The next `text(day)` when the rooster marched by and announced loudly, “Efo eve!” (“It's `text(two)` o'clock!”), Mr. Agbele again called, “Friend Rooster!”
“What is it, Friend Man?” answered the rooster. “Please don't ask me to give up my watch. Everyone depends on me to announce the time.”

“I merely wanted to suggest that you announce the time on the other side of the village,” said Mr. Agbele. “You see, when I am studying my books, I have no need to know the `text(hour)`. I know it is time to eat when my stomach growls. I fall asleep with the setting of the sun. So perhaps you could use your wonderful gift elsewhere.”
The rooster clucked impatiently and said, “How selfish you are! Perhaps you do not appreciate the service I perform, but I assure you that your neighbors do. Good `text(day)`, Friend Man.”

Poor Mr. Agbele didn't know what to do. He tried stuffing cotton in his ears, he tried wrapping his head in cloth, he tried closing all the shutters in his house. Nothing could keep out the blaring of the rooster's `text(hourly)` announcements.

Finally, Mr. Agbele could stand it no longer. `text(One)` afternoon, just when he was puzzling over a particularly difficult passage in `text(one)` of his books, the rooster's “Efo eto!” (“It's `text(three)` o'clock!”) scattered his thoughts like leaves in the wind.

“Friend Rooster!” he shouted angrily through the window. “I have read that time flies when a person is enjoying himself. Thanks to you, for me time crawls like a worm, like a snail! I am truly at my wits' end!”

But the rooster heard only Mr. Agbele's `text(first)` few words. Time flies! “Of course!” thought the rooster. “Why didn't I think of it sooner? `text(Every hour)`, I will fly over the whole village announcing the time. Soon everyone in the village will know what a clever rooster I am! What a marvelous plan!”
At `text(four)` o'clock, the rooster flapped his wings furiously and launched himself into the air. “Efo en -” he crowed.

Unfortunately, the rooster had forgotten `text(two)` things - `text(one)`, that he had the habit of throwing back his head and closing his eyes when he crowed, and `text(two)`, that roosters, as a rule, do not fly very high, especially when wearing heavy pocket watches. So just as he began to crow, head back and eyes closed, the large baobab tree in Mr. Agbele's yard jumped right in his path. They collided with an awful confusion of feathers, squawks, and broken branches. Then down fell the rooster with a thud.
Mr. Agbele rushed out and found him lying in the dust, the breath knocked out of him, pieces of the shattered watch on `text(every side)`.
Gently Mr. Agbele took the rooster inside. He spent a `text(week)` feeding the poor bird corn broth and bathing his head with a cool towel until he was well again.

After that, the rooster still crowed at daybreak to wake Mr. Agbele. The rest of the `text(day)` he marched back and forth, asking, “Ga nene efo? Ga nene efo?” of everyone he met. Mr. Agbele became so accustomed to the question that he hardly heard it.
But to this `text(day)`, descendants of the rooster remember their clever ancestor, and they still ask, “Ga nene efo?” “What time is it?”
